faq: Do we need a permit for photos in Stanley Park?

For a wedding or engagement photo session with no special setup — no arches, chairs or decorations — the Vancouver Park Board doesn't require a permit. If you plan a setup, you'll need a photography permit, and a wedding ceremony needs a separate ceremony permit.
What's the best time of day for photos in Stanley Park?

The hour before sunset. Third Beach and the western seawall face the sunset over English Bay, and the forest and Lost Lagoon glow in the low light. Early morning is lovely too, with calm water and almost no crowds.
Can we get married in Stanley Park?

Yes. Small stand-up ceremonies are allowed at the Park Board's designated wedding locations with a ceremony permit. Apply at least four weeks ahead — the 2026 outdoor wedding season runs from March 1 to September 30.

Stanley Park has pay parking throughout. For engagement sessions I usually suggest meeting near the Rose Garden and Pavilion, then driving or walking to the seawall and Third Beach for sunset. Summer weekends are busy, so allow extra time.
prose:
Stanley Park is Vancouver's most-loved place for wedding and engagement photos — and for good reason. In one park you have the seawall, ocean sunsets, a rose garden, a lagoon with willows and fountains, quiet forest trails and views of the Lions Gate Bridge and the North Shore mountains.

I'm Joenell, a Vancouver wedding and engagement photographer. This guide covers the best photo spots in Stanley Park, when the light is best, a simple session route, and what to know about permits and parking.

Why Couples Love Stanley Park

Stanley Park gives you a huge variety of backgrounds within a few minutes of each other — water, forest, gardens and city views — so even a short session feels like several locations. It's also right next to downtown, which makes it easy to fit portraits into a wedding day at a downtown hotel or venue.

The Best Photo Spots in Stanley Park

The seawall

The seawall loops around the whole park. The western side, between Siwash Rock and Third Beach, faces the sunset and has open ocean with the mountains behind. Near Brockton Point you get the little lighthouse and views back to the city and Coal Harbour.

Third Beach and Second Beach

Third Beach is my favourite sunset spot in the park: soft sand, driftwood and the sun dropping into English Bay. Second Beach is a little busier but easy to reach and lovely at golden hour.

Lost Lagoon

At the park entrance, Lost Lagoon has a fountain, weeping willows and a calm path around the water — great for relaxed walking photos and soft reflections.

The Stanley Park Rose Garden

Near the Pavilion, the Rose Garden blooms from late spring through summer, with arbours and pathways that make beautiful frames for wedding and engagement portraits.

Ted and Mary Greig Rhododendron Garden

In April and May this quiet garden near the pitch-and-putt bursts with rhododendrons and azaleas — one of the prettiest spring backdrops in Vancouver.

Prospect Point

The lookout at the north end of the park gives you a classic view of the Lions Gate Bridge and the North Shore — best on a clear day.

Forest trails and Beaver Lake

The trails through the middle of the park have tall cedars, ferns and soft, even light — perfect on cloudy days or in the middle of the afternoon. Beaver Lake adds lily pads and a peaceful, hidden feel.

A note on the totem poles at Brockton Point: they're cultural works of the Coast Salish and other First Nations. I photograph couples nearby with the view of the harbour rather than posing with the poles themselves.

The Best Time of Day and Season

For most sessions I plan around the hour before sunset, when the light is soft and warm and the seawall glows.

  • Summer: sunset is around 9:20 pm in late June, so evening sessions start after dinner.
  • Winter: sunset is around 4:15 pm in December — plan an early-afternoon session.
  • Spring: cherry blossoms and rhododendrons from March to May.
  • Autumn: golden leaves along the trails and around Lost Lagoon in October.

Early mornings are wonderful too: calm water, soft light and an almost empty seawall. Read more in the best time of year for engagement photos in Vancouver.

A Sample Engagement Session Route

  • Start: the Rose Garden and the paths near the Pavilion — relaxed, warm-up photos.
  • Next: Lost Lagoon for willows, water and walking shots.
  • Finish: Third Beach or the western seawall for golden hour and sunset.

A 60–90 minute session comfortably covers two or three of these spots. For a surprise proposal, the seawall near Siwash Rock and Third Beach are quieter choices than English Bay.

Permits for Photos and Ceremonies

According to the Vancouver Park Board, wedding photos in a park don't need a permit as long as there's no special setup. If you'd like a setup — an arch, chairs, signage or décor — you'll need a photography permit.

A wedding ceremony needs a ceremony permit and must be held at one of the Park Board's designated wedding locations. Ceremonies are small and stand-up, applications need at least four weeks' notice, and the 2026 season runs from March 1 to September 30. Restaurants and event venues inside the park handle their own bookings. I'll help you check what applies to your plans.

Parking and Practical Tips

  • Parking: pay parking throughout the park; arrive 15 minutes early on summer weekends.
  • Shoes: bring comfortable shoes for walking between spots and change for photos.
  • Crowds: the seawall is busy on sunny afternoons — I'll guide you to quieter corners.
  • Rain: the forest canopy keeps you drier, and a clear umbrella makes lovely rainy-day portraits.
  • Outfits: see what to wear for engagement photos in Vancouver.

Pricing

Engagement sessions start at $225, surprise proposals at $250, elopements at $850 and weddings at $1,000. Stanley Park is in Vancouver, so there's no travel charge. See all the details on the pricing page, or browse more ideas in 20 beautiful photo locations in Vancouver.
